data.rationale: FND-006 states the whole core insight. ACQ-TH1's file arrives at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT. Matching and report generation then take 60 minutes, so reports publish at about 08:30 SGT, after the 08:00 SGT deadline in NFR-8. It also says 2027 volume is about twice the 2025 level. Its locations (16.2, NFR-8) overlap the flaw's. The other findings that cite NFR-8 or nearby sections cover different defects. For example, FND-007 cites NFR-8 only for the auto-match target, not the publication deadline.

FND-005 is the only finding that states the core insight. It says NFR-4 requires zero RPO even if a whole region is lost, and that Section 20.2's cross-region replication is asynchronous with lag under one second, so commits in that window are lost on unplanned failover. It cites NFR-4, Section 2.2 and Section 20.2. FND-010 and FND-018 only mention NFR-4 in passing (game-day sequencing, and a pointer to FND-005), so neither describes the replication contradiction.

FND-002 is the only finding that describes this defect. It covers Section 13.1, where the Fraud Hook detokenises the PAN using the Card Adapter's role and sends it to FRV-1. It says this contradicts P2, Section 12.1 and Section 12.2, which places the Fraud Hook outside CDE scope. It also notes that sharing the service role breaks P9, and it ties the problem to NFR-5. FND-016 also mentions FRV-1, but only for personal data and privacy (NFR-7), not the CDE boundary. FND-004 is about keeping the CVC, which is a different defect.

FND-012 targets Section 9.3's 10,000-WCU-per-partition claim and the merchant_id hot key for the largest merchant. It also covers the ignored 4 KB item size and the LSI item-collection limit, but it calls the limit unverified rather than stating 1,000 WCU. FND-013 only mentions unhandled DynamoDB throttling, so it is weakly related.

FND-011 is the only finding that states F05's core insight. It says Section 21.1's '<1% of card payments cascade' premise contradicts the 3.8% retryable rate in Section 10.5. It notes that a 2,500 ms timeout on its own goes past the 1,500 ms limit. It also concludes that NFR-2 would likely fail its own acceptance test. FND-003 covers the same cascade-after-timeout area in Section 11.2, but its defect is different: it is about double authorizations, not latency. I've kept it only as a weak second candidate. No other finding deals with the latency budget.

FND-016 is the only finding that matches this flaw. It cites NFR-7 and Section 19.1, notes that data from all markets is processed in Singapore with disaster recovery in Jakarta, and says it is unverified whether Indonesian or other rules require local processing. That covers the missing residency requirement, Indonesia's exposure and the need for regulatory confirmation. It sits inside a broader privacy-inventory finding, so it may score PARTIAL rather than MATCH. Other findings that share locations with the flaw (FND-005, FND-004, FND-006 and FND-014) describe unrelated defects: recovery point, retention of card security codes, reconciliation timing and network tokens.

FND-009 is the only finding that matches this flaw. It says MFA is optional for Finance (18.3) and that Finance can change the payout account (18.2/18.4) with no step-up, second approver or owner notification. It also says only the person who made the change gets the confirmation email, so a phished Finance password could redirect all of a merchant's payouts unnoticed. That covers the flaw's core point and cites the same sections. FND-014 also cites section 24, but it is about network tokens and is a different defect.

FND-004 is the only finding about keeping the CVC. It cites Section 12.4 and NFR-6 and the claim about PCI DSS 3.2.1 and 3.3.2. It covers keeping the CVC until settlement or for 72 hours and using it for incremental authorizations after the authorization has completed. It also raises the reading that bans keeping sensitive authentication data after authorization. It hedges by calling the reading unverified. The other findings cover unrelated defects.

FND-001 states the full core insight in substance. The Redis key idem:resp:{idempotency_key} has no merchant_id and is checked first (Section 9.2). Section 9.1 accepts merchants' own order and invoice IDs as keys, so collisions between merchants are likely. A collision leaks the first merchant's payment data, and the second merchant's payment is never created. The finding also says this breaks P3 and FR-5. FND-018 is a much weaker candidate: it only mentions that the FR-5 acceptance test does not cover cross-merchant key reuse, and refers back to FND-001. The other idempotency finding, FND-013, covers a different defect: orphaned locks and keys expiring after 24 hours.

FND-008 is the only finding that describes this defect. It names a single CloudHSM in ap-southeast-1a as a single point of failure. It also says DEKs aren't cached, so every detokenise needs the HSM. It notes the clash with the three-AZ posture in Section 20.1 and with NFR-3, and that the 1,500 TPS trigger never fires because the design peak is 1,100 TPS. FND-020 mentions the HSM capacity trigger only as a process with no named owner. FND-002 and FND-014 are about other defects.

FND-018 makes the same point as F13. It cites the anchor quote from 26.1 and says the FR-5 test only resends after the first response arrives, so it never tests the concurrent duplicates that FR-5 explicitly names. FND-013 is only a weak fallback: it covers idempotency failure paths such as orphaned IN_PROGRESS locks, which are on the same topic but are a different defect. The other findings are about different things, for example FND-001, which is about the Redis key not being scoped to the merchant.

FND-003 states the core insight. It cites sections 11.1 and 11.2 and quotes the anchor claim that cascading cannot create a duplicate charge. It covers all three required points: a timeout is treated as retryable although the first attempt may have been approved, a late approval plus a second approval authorises the customer twice, and late responses are discarded with no reversal, leaving an orphaned authorization. The other findings in the location hint describe different defects. FND-008 covers the HSM single point of failure and the Vault 503 mapping, FND-013 covers idempotency locks and the sweeper, FND-015 covers scheme limits, and FND-011 covers the latency budget.

FND-014 matches the core insight. It says network tokens are a confirmed decision from launch (AD-010, Section 24) and that Phase 3 is rated 'No - ready'. It also says Backlog item 2 shows the TRID registration, the token-service-provider agreement and certification have not started, so the decision and the readiness rating are overstated. FND-015 cites Section 27 but is about the Retry Engine's scheme limits, which is a different defect. No other finding covers network tokens.

FND-017 directly says FR-8's 2% and the 10.3 tolerance have no defined unit (percentage points vs relative). It cites FR-8, 10.3 and 26.1, and quotes the weekly Routing Review text, which touches the per-transaction vs merchant-level reading. FND-020 cites 10.3's weekly review but is about missing owners, so it is only a weak backup.

The finding states the core insight in full. It gives the time-zone conversion ("ACQ-TH1's file lands at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT"). It gives the timing arithmetic ("matcher plus report generation take 60 minutes ... earliest publication is 08:30 SGT even at today's volume"), which misses the NFR-8 deadline. It covers growth ("2027 daily attempts are about twice the 2025 level"). Read with "even at today's volume", that last point clearly means the delay gets worse, though the finding does not say "later" outright. The cut-off and partial-run point is extra and does not take away from the match. The finding cites sections 16.2 and 2.2 and NFR-8, which overlap the key flaw's location.

The finding states the whole timing argument. On the time-zone conversion it says "ACQ-TH1's file lands at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT". On the arithmetic it says "matcher plus report generation take 60 minutes ... so the earliest publication is 08:30 SGT even at today's volume", which misses the NFR-8 08:00 SGT target. On growth it says "2027 daily attempts are about twice the 2025 level", which says in substance that the gap gets worse. It also names the cause, that the matcher "starts only after every file for day T has arrived". The locations, section 16.2, section 2.2 and NFR-8, overlap the flaw's locations. The finding does not criticise batch reconciliation as such, so the distractor does not apply. The extra point about a missing file blocking the run is additional and does not reduce the match.

This is a full match. The finding says that in 13.1 the Fraud Hook will "detokenise the full card number using the Card Adapter's client library and service role, and send it to the third-party vendor FRV-1" (c1, c4). It says this contradicts 12.2, "which scopes the Fraud Hook out of the CDE with 'Token, BIN, last 4 only'", as well as P2 and 12.1 (c2). For the consequence, it says "the NFR-5 assessment against the Section 12.2 CDE boundary would not hold as written, and FRV-1 would receive cardholder data". That covers the core insight: the declared CDE boundary is wrong and the vendor handles cardholder data (c3). The finding never literally says "the Fraud Hook is in PCI scope", but the substance is there. Its locations (13.1, 12.1, 12.2, NFR-5) overlap the key flaw's locations.

This is a full match. The finding states the core mechanism: in Section 13.1 the Fraud Hook "detokenise[s] the full card number using the Card Adapter's client library and service role, and send[s] it to the third-party vendor FRV-1" (c1, c4). It says this contradicts P2 and "Section 12.2, which scopes the Fraud Hook out of the CDE with 'Token, BIN, last 4 only'" (c2). It also gives the consequence: "The NFR-5 assessment against the Section 12.2 CDE boundary would not hold as written, and FRV-1 would receive cardholder data" (c3). It never literally says "the Fraud Hook is in the CDE" or names FRV-1 a third-party service provider, but it does say the declared boundary is wrong and that a third party receives cardholder data. That covers the substance of the core insight. The finding cites 13.1, 12.1, 12.2 and NFR-5, which overlap the flaw's location.

The finding states the whole core insight. On c1, it says "NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings on loss of an AWS region". On c2, it says the only cross-region copy "is asynchronous with 'typical lag under one second'". On c3, it says "commits inside the lag window are lost on unplanned failover" and that "the NFR-4 game day cannot demonstrate zero loss". It cites sections 2.2 and 20.2 and NFR-4, which overlap the flaw's location. The extra point about rebuilding idempotency state does not weaken the match.

The finding states that NFR-4 requires "zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings on loss of an AWS region". It also says the cross-region copy "is asynchronous with 'typical lag under one second', so commits inside the lag window are lost on unplanned failover", and that the "NFR-4 game day cannot demonstrate zero loss". The extra point about idempotency reconstruction does not reduce the match.

The finding is located correctly. It quotes the "single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units" anchor in section 9.3 and cites NFR-1. It identifies the right defect area. It states the hot-key consequence (c2): "the largest merchant's idempotency writes will throttle on campaign days, causing failed payments for 45% of peak traffic". It also states the c3 points: the count "ignores item size, even though response_body is up to 4 KB" and ignores "any item-collection size constraint from the LSI". However, it never says the claimed limit is wrong or gives the actual limit of 1,000 WCU per partition. It only says "The register cannot confirm that per-partition limit" and "If the real limits are lower". The core insight is that the 10,000 figure is wrong by 10x and the true limit is 1,000 WCU, so even 1,800 WCU is already over it. The finding leaves that as a hypothetical, so the core insight is only partly stated and c1 is missing. That makes this a PARTIAL match rather than a full one.

The finding cites §9.2 and FR-5, so its location overlaps the flaw's. The defect it describes is different, though. It covers orphan IN_PROGRESS locks that the AUTHORISING-only sweeper misses, missing handling for a DynamoDB outage ("Section 20.4 covers a Redis outage but not DynamoDB unavailability or throttling, so it is undefined whether the API fails open... or fails closed"), and order-ID reuse after the 24-hour expiry. It never says the 10,000 WCU per-partition figure is wrong (the real limit is 1,000 WCU). It never names merchant_id as the hot partition key for M-0001's ~900 TPS. It also never mentions the item-size WCU cost or the LSI. The single mention of "throttling" is about failure-mode handling, not the capacity miscalculation. The distractor notes say that even a bare "DynamoDB may throttle" is partial at best, and here it isn't even the claim being made. The finding is in the same area but describes a different defect, so the score is RELATED.

The finding cites Section 9.2 and FR-5, which overlap the flaw's location. It describes a different defect, though: idempotency failure paths. It names three of them: orphan IN_PROGRESS locks the sweeper misses, an undefined fail-open or fail-closed behaviour on "DynamoDB unavailability or throttling", and reuse of order IDs after 24 hours. It never says that the 10,000 WCU per-partition figure is wrong (the real limit is 1,000). It never says that keying the table by merchant_id makes M-0001's ~900 TPS a hot partition. It also never mentions WCU item-size costs or the LSI. The only overlap is the bare mention of throttling, and the distractor notes say this earns at most partial credit when the wrong number and the hot key are not named. So the pair is RELATED: the same area, but a different mechanism.

The finding targets the right claim in section 9.3, quoting "single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units per second". But it only calls the limit unverified ("The register cannot confirm that per-partition limit"; "If the real limits are lower") and never says the actual limit is 1,000 WCU, so c1 is missing. It does state the hot-key effect: "the largest merchant's idempotency writes will throttle on campaign days... 45% of peak traffic" (c2). It also says the write count "ignores item size, even though response_body is up to 4 KB" and ignores the "item-collection size constraint from the LSI" (c3). Location 9.3 / NFR-1 is compatible. The core insight is hedged rather than stated, so this is a partial match.

The finding cites Section 11.2, which is one of the flaw's locations, and it covers the same cascade-and-timeout mechanics. But it describes a different defect: a duplicate charge. It says a "late approval leaves a live authorization hold on the customer's card at the first acquirer while the second acquirer also approves" and that "cascading cannot create a duplicate charge" does not hold. It says nothing about the p99 latency budget, the "<1% cascade" premise, the 3.8% retryable rate in Section 10.5, or NFR-2's 1,500 ms target being missed. None of the credit items c1, c2 or c3 is stated (it mentions the 2,500 ms timeout, but not as a cost to latency). This is the right area with the wrong mechanism, so it scores RELATED.

This is a match. The finding states the contradiction directly: Section 21.1 drops cascades from the budget "because 'fewer than 1% of card payments cascade', yet Section 10.5 gives 3.8% retryable outcomes and the NFR-2 test injects 3.8%" (c1). It gives the cost mechanism: "Any attempt that hits the 2,500 ms timeout already exceeds NFR-2's 1,500 ms on its own" (c2). It draws the conclusion that "NFR-2 is likely to fail its own acceptance test" (c3). It never says outright that the 99th percentile falls among cascaded payments, and it adds an "or it is ambiguous" hedge. Even so, the core insight is present in substance. The cited locations, Sections 21.1 and 10.5 and NFR-2, overlap the key flaw's locations. The finding does not lean on either distractor: it neither disputes the 238 ms arithmetic nor calls the fraud timeout too long.

The finding states the contradiction: Section 21.1 excludes cascades "because 'fewer than 1% of card payments cascade', yet Section 10.5 gives 3.8% retryable outcomes and the NFR-2 test injects 3.8%" (c1). It covers the cost of cascading: "Any attempt that hits the 2,500 ms timeout already exceeds NFR-2's 1,500 ms on its own" (c2). It concludes that "NFR-2 is likely to fail its own acceptance test" (c3). It does not say outright that the p99 falls inside the cascaded population, but this is clearly implied, and the "or ambiguous" hedge is minor. Its locations (21.1, 10.5, NFR-2) overlap the key flaw's locations. The extra 3DS remark is a separate point and does not count against the match.

The finding and the flaw both involve cascading and the 2,500 ms timeout in Section 11.2, but they describe different defects. The finding is about correctness: late approvals are "logged against the attempt and discarded", which leaves "a live authorization hold" and a possible double authorisation with "no reversal message". It never mentions latency, the p99 budget, NFR-2, Section 21.1's "<1% cascade" premise or the 3.8% retryable rate in Section 10.5. None of the credit items c1–c3 is stated. Section 11.2 is one of the flaw's locations, so the location overlaps, but the mechanism is wrong. That caps the score at RELATED.

The finding targets the right defect and location: NFR-6 and Section 12.4 keep the encrypted CVC "until settlement or for up to 72 hours". It also notes that incremental authorizations "happen after the initial authorization has completed". It never states the core insight, though. It does not say that 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 fail to permit this, and it does not cite Req. 3.3.1 or 3.3.1.2. It only raises non-compliance as a possibility: "If a QSA reads the standard as prohibiting retention of sensitive authentication data after authorization…". It also says outright that it "cannot confirm or refute the clause and treats it as unverified." Because the core insight is hedged and not asserted, none of the credit items are clearly stated, so this is PARTIAL, not MATCH.

This is the same defect at the right location: §12.4, §2.2 and NFR-6, with the anchor quote cited. The finding points out that incremental authorizations "happen after the initial authorization has completed". It also raises the possibility that "a QSA reads the standard as prohibiting retention of sensitive authentication data after authorization". However, it never says that the cited clauses fail to allow this, or that PCI DSS Req. 3.3.1 / 3.3.1.2 forbids keeping the CVC after authorization even when encrypted. Instead it says "This review cannot confirm or refute the clause and treats it as unverified." It treats the problem as a missing source rather than as non-compliance. So c1, c2 and c3 are only raised as possibilities and never asserted. The topic and mechanism are correct, but the core insight is only partly stated. That makes this a PARTIAL match.

Partial match (score 2). The locations line up: the finding cites sections 2.2 and 19.1 and NFR-7, which are the flaw's own locations. It states c2: the design "processes all markets' data in Singapore with DR in Jakarta". It partly states c3: "whether Indonesian or other rules require local processing is unverified in the register". However, the finding is mainly about privacy inventory, purpose and retention mapping, and transfer basis under NFR-7. It treats local processing as one gap among several privacy gaps. It never says that no data-residency or localisation requirement exists, or that NFR-7 covers privacy only (c1). It also doesn't point to Indonesia's position as the largest market, or say that the single-region data placement may need structural change. So the same defect is present, but the core insight is only partly stated.

The finding mainly covers a privacy and retention inventory under NFR-7. It does state that the design "processes all markets' data in Singapore with DR in Jakarta" (c2) and that "whether Indonesian or other rules require local processing is unverified in the register" (c3, briefly). It never says that no residency or localisation requirement exists or that NFR-7 is privacy-only (c1). It frames the issue as a privacy "transfer basis" gap and does not call for possibly changing the data placement. Same defect but only partly stated. The location (2.2, 19.1, NFR-7) overlaps the flaw's location.

The finding states the whole core insight. On MFA it says "MFA is optional for Finance (Section 18.3)" and quotes the rule that MFA is enforced only for Owner. On the bank account change it notes the change "lacks step-up MFA, a second approver" and that Finance can change the payout account. On the fraud risk it says "A phished Finance password alone can redirect all of a merchant's payouts, and the only alert goes to the attacker." It also cites the P9 conflict. Its locations (18.2, 18.3, 18.4, FR-13) overlap the flaw's locations. It does not mention the missing cooling-off period, but the credit rule is substance, so this does not reduce the score.

This finding describes the same defect as F08, and its location matches: sections 18.2, 18.3 and 18.4 and FR-13. All three parts of the core insight are stated. On MFA, it says "MFA is optional for Finance (Section 18.3)" and quotes "enforced for the Owner role at first login". The finding describes the same defect and states the core insight in full. On c1 it says the fast path is keyed "idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, with no merchant_id" and that this "breaks P3 and FR-5". On c2 it says "Section 9.1 accepts order and invoice numbers as keys. Two merchants that reuse the same order number within 24 hours will collide." This finding is about gaps in the acceptance tests. Its only mention of the topic is that the FR-5 test never exercises "concurrent duplicates ... or cross-merchant key reuse (see FND-001)". It never says that the Redis fast-path key idem:resp:{idempotency_key} leaves out merchant_id (c1). It also doesn't say collisions are likely because merchants use their own order IDs as keys (c2), or that one merchant gets another merchant's stored response and its own payment is never processed (c3). The FR-5 ID overlaps, so the location is compatible. But the defect it describes is missing test coverage, not the Redis key-scoping bug. The details are deferred to FND-001, so the score is RELATED.

This finding is about weak acceptance tests. For FR-5 it only says the test "never exercises the concurrent duplicates ... or cross-merchant key reuse (see FND-001)". This is a full match. The finding focuses on timeouts and covers 5xx only through its 11.1 quote. That is enough because the core mechanism, an ambiguous outcome cascaded with no reversal, is fully stated.

The finding states the core insight. It says FR-8's '2%' and the 'tolerance (default 2)' in Section 10.3 have "undefined units". It also says "Percentage points and a relative 2% differ materially (on an 88% baseline, 2 points is about 2.3% relative)". The finding states it: FR-8's "2%" and the "tolerance (default 2)" are "undefined units". It also says "Percentage points and a relative 2% differ materially (on an 88% baseline, 2 points is about 2.3% relative)", and notes that "The FR-8 test checks only expected choices and does not probe the bound". Together these give the defect: the rule can be read two ways, and the acceptance test does not settle which reading applies.
