Because c3 is marked "and/or", that gap does not block the match. The locations (2.1/FR-8, 10.3, 26.1) overlap the flaw's locations.

The finding states the core insight in substance: "The FR-5 test resends only after the first response has arrived, so it never exercises the concurrent duplicates that FR-5 names explicitly." This covers c1 (FR-5 requires concurrent duplicate handling) and c2 (the test is a sequential replay that cannot validate concurrency). It also points out the missing cross-merchant case, which matches the key's note about F09. It does not explicitly propose parallel injection or a 409 assertion (c3). That omission does not cost credit, because this flaw's credit rule is "substance" and the credit items are guidance only. The cited location (26.1, FR-5) and the quoted anchor text match the key flaw exactly. The other parts of the finding, on FR-12 and NFR-9, do not take away from this match.

The finding covers FR-5 idempotency in Section 9, so its location overlaps the flaw's. Its defect is different, though: unspecified failure paths. It describes orphan IN_PROGRESS locks the sweeper never clears ("Section 20.3 scans only payments in AUTHORISING"), undefined fail-open or fail-closed behaviour when DynamoDB is down, and "a merchant retry after the 24-hour expiry creates a second charge". It never mentions the FR-5 acceptance criterion (Section 26.1). It also never says the test replays the duplicate only after the first response arrives, so a broken concurrency lock could not be detected, or that parallel duplicate injection is needed. The finding touches the same area (IN_PROGRESS locks and 409s), but the mechanism differs, so the score is RELATED.

The finding and the flaw share a location: both cite FR-5 and Section 9 (9.1 and 9.2). But the finding describes a different defect. It covers gaps in the idempotency design: orphaned locks ("Section 20.3 scans only payments in AUTHORISING", leaving "a key that returns 409 for up to 24 hours"), DynamoDB unavailability ("fails open... or fails closed"), and order-ID keys reused after the 24-hour expiry. The flaw is about the FR-5 acceptance test in Section 26.1, which "resends the identical request" only "after its response is received". Because that replay is sequential, it cannot detect a broken concurrency lock. The finding never mentions the acceptance criterion, never says the test is sequential, and never asks for parallel duplicate injection. So c1, c2 and c3 are all absent. It is the same topic area with a different mechanism, so the score is RELATED (1).

The finding states that "The FR-5 test resends only after the first response has arrived, so it never exercises the concurrent duplicates that FR-5 names explicitly." This captures the core insight that a sequential replay cannot validate the concurrency FR-5 requires (c1, c2). It does not propose parallel injection or a 409 assertion (c3). The credit rule is substance, so c3 is guidance only, and the mechanism is fully stated. The location matches section 26.1 / FR-5 and uses the exact anchor quote. The extra FR-12 and NFR-9 content does not affect this pair.

This is a full match. The finding gives both sides of the contradiction. On the decision side, it says network tokens are confirmed "primary card-on-file credential from launch, and Phase 3 is marked 'No - ready'" (c1). On the dependency side, it says "Backlog item 2 shows the Token Requestor registration, the commercial agreement and certification are not yet started" (c2). It then draws the conclusion that "the confirmed decision and the readiness rating are not true at launch" (c3). Its cited location, Section 24 / FR-14, appears in the flaw's location list. It does not fall into the distractor: it does not object to FR-14's wording, only to the confirmed and ready status.

The finding states each part of the core insight. For c1, it says "AD-010 makes VTS and MDES network tokens the primary card-on-file credential from launch, and Phase 3 is marked 'No - ready'". For c2, it says "Backlog item 2 shows the Token Requestor registration, the commercial agreement and certification are not yet started". For c3, it says "the confirmed decision and the readiness rating are not true at launch". The finding cites Section 24 and FR-14 and uses the anchor quote, so its location overlaps the flaw's location. It also refers to Phase 3 and backlog item 2. It does not rely on FR-14's 'where the issuer supports' wording, which the distractor notes exclude.

The main premise holds. In §7.2, CAPTURED and SUCCEEDED can move to PARTIALLY_REFUNDED or REFUNDED. From there the only allowed move is PARTIALLY_REFUNDED to REFUNDED, and nothing leads from either state to SETTLED. §16.2, however, says "Matched payments transition to SETTLED". So a payment refunded before its settlement line arrives cannot be settled without breaking FR-2. This also matters for §12.4, which deletes the CVC when a payment reaches SETTLED. The point about partial capture also holds. FR-1 requires partial capture, but §7.2 has no CAPTURED to CAPTURED transition, so a payment can only be captured once, and the document doesn't say how the uncaptured remainder is released. The memo-ledger point is weaker, because §8 step 10 says "(authorization memo)", which fits with §14.3. Still, the central state-machine defect is specific, grounded in the document and real. No key flaw (F01–F14) or observation covers it, and none of the review's other findings raise it.

The premise holds. Section 28 puts the first cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) live after Phase 7. The Fraud Hook is Phase 8, still blocked on the FRV-1 contract (Backlog item 4), and the PCI DSS assessment, load tests and DR game days are Phase 9. FR-9 requires every card payment to be scored before authorization, so launch cards would breach FR-9 and go live before NFR-5, NFR-1, NFR-2 and NFR-4 are validated. Section 27's conclusion names only the Admin API schemas and the dispute module as non-blocking gaps. The issue is specific to this document, is not among the key flaws (F14 is about network tokens) and is not raised by any other finding.

The premise checks out. Section 11.3 only says the engine stops 'at the scheme limits applicable to the card' and never states the limits, the source rule set, or whether a cross-acquirer cascade counts as a reattempt. Yet Section 27 rates the Retry Engine 'Ready' and claims the 'scheme rules specified (Section 11)', and the FR-7 test in Section 26.1 checks limits the document never defines. This is a real readiness and testability gap. It differs from F10 (timeout cascade with no reversal) and matches no other key flaw or observation. No other finding in the review raises it (FND-003 covers timeouts, FND-018 covers other test criteria).

The premises mostly hold. §20.4 covers 'Redis down' but not DynamoDB being unavailable or throttled, so fail-open versus fail-closed is undefined. §9.1 accepts order and invoice IDs as keys, and 'a request after expiry is treated as new', so a merchant retry after 24 hours can create a second charge. On orphan locks, §20.3 does say the sweeper 'also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS', so 'scans only AUTHORISING' is overstated. However, the only resolution mechanism described works on AUTHORISING payments, and §9.2's 'resolves the payment' does not cover a pod crash before the payment exists or while it is in CREATED. This is distinct from FND-001 (Redis keys not merchant-scoped), FND-012 (DynamoDB partition capacity), FND-005 (idempotency rebuild after regional failover) and key flaws F04 and F09.

The premise holds. FR-15 sends refunds as a bank payout to "the customer's nominated account", but no section says how that account is collected, verified or protected, or how the refund payout is journaled (Section 14.2 shows only capture, settlement and merchant payout journals). Section 16.3 subtracts "reserves and pending dispute holds" without defining them, and no rule covers a negative merchant_payable. Section 27 still rates Payouts "Ready". Dispute case management is out of scope, but Sections 1 and 25 put dispute ledger events in v1, so their effect on payouts is in scope, and the finding acknowledges the backlog item. The key does not list this gap, and no other finding covers it: FND-007 is about the state machine and memo ledger, and FND-016 is about privacy retention.

The finding's facts are true: Section 10.3 describes a weekly Routing Review with no named owner, and the title page lists the PCI DSS Scoping Memo as a draft. But its complaint, that operational processes lack named owners and SLAs and the document lacks change control, is generic governance advice that would fit almost any design. The finding itself says "none of this causes failure by itself". It names no concrete technical defect in this design, and it does not show any error caused by the draft memo it mentions.

data.doc_passage: On completion of a request, the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL. On every incoming mutating request, the Payments API checks this key first; on a hit, it returns the stored response immediately without touching DynamoDB or the Orchestrator.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 9.2 keys the Redis fast path on idem:resp:{idempotency_key} alone, with no merchant_id, and returns the stored response on a hit before any DynamoDB lookup or request-hash comparison. Section 9.1 also accepts merchant order and invoice identifiers as keys.
data.rationale: The document matches what the finding says. Section 9.2 keys the Redis entry only on idempotency_key, with no merchant_id, and on a hit it returns the cached response without going to DynamoDB, where the request_hash check happens. Section 9.1 says: "merchants frequently use their own order or invoice identifiers, which is accepted." The quoted text appears as given. Section 24 repeats the key format as idem:resp:{key}.

data.doc_passage: FRV-1's consortium velocity graph is keyed on the full card number, which allows it to link the same card across its other clients in the region; scoring quality falls materially without it. The Fraud Hook obtains the PAN through the Vault's detokenise operation, using the Card Adapter client library and service role.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 13.1 has the Fraud Hook detokenise the full PAN using the Card Adapter's client library and service role and send it to FRV-1. This conflicts with P2, with Section 12.1 (only the Card Adapter may detokenise) and with Section 12.2 (Fraud Hook is out of the CDE scope with 'Token, BIN, last 4 only'), and the FRV-1 contract/DPA is still pending.
data.rationale: The finding is supported. In Section 13.1, the payload table lists "card_number" with source "Vault detokenise", and the text says the Fraud Hook gets the PAN through the Card Adapter's client library and service role. Each conflicting passage the finding cites is in the document as quoted: P2 says PAN leaves the Vault only over the Card Adapter's connection to an acquirer; Section 12.1 says "Only the Card Adapter's service identity may call detokenise"; and Section 12.2 lists "Fraud Hook Out of scope Token, BIN, last 4 only". Backlog item 4 confirms that the FRV-1 data processing agreement (DPA) and SLA are still pending.

data.doc_passage: The CVC is required for the initial customer-initiated authorization and, at several acquirers, for each re-presentation of the credential during a cascade and for incremental authorizations (ride-hailing tips, hotel extensions). The Vault therefore stores the CVC encrypted under a separate KEK, and deletes it when the Reconciliation Service marks the associated payment SETTLED, or after 72 hours, whichever is first. This is permitted by PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2, which allow sensitive authentication data to be retained in encrypted form until the transaction is settled.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document keeps the encrypted CVC until settlement or for up to 72 hours, including for incremental authorizations, and asserts that PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow retaining sensitive authentication data until the transaction is settled. The companion PCI DSS Scoping Memo is listed as a draft.
data.rationale: The document says what the finding claims. Section 12.4 says the CVC is stored encrypted until settlement or for at most 72 hours. It says the CVC is used for cascades and incremental authorizations, and it cites 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 as allowing retention until settlement. NFR-6 says the same thing, and the cover page lists the "PCI DSS Scoping Memo (draft)". "AD-009" and the "evidence register" come from the review itself, not the document. They don't change whether the finding describes the document correctly.

data.doc_passage: Because each attempt carries its own attempt_id and the previous attempt did not succeed, cascading cannot create a duplicate charge: the ledger records only the approved attempt. Responses that arrive for an attempt after its 2,500 ms timeout are logged against the attempt and discarded.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The design cascades to the next acquirer after a 2,500 ms timeout and discards any late response from the first acquirer. It specifies no reversal or void of a late-approved authorization at the first acquirer, yet still claims that cascading cannot create a duplicate charge.
data.rationale:
All three quoted passages are in the document. Section 11.1 lists "no response within 2,500 ms" as retryable. Section 11.2 says late responses are "logged against the attempt and discarded" and claims cascading "cannot create a duplicate charge."

I searched for a reversal or void at the attempt level and found none. The only voids are at the payment level: the AUTHORISED→CANCELLED transition and the expiry sweeper. Both apply to the payment's single winning authorization, not to an orphaned earlier attempt. The stuck-payment sweeper only handles payments still in AUTHORISING. Reconciliation matches settlement lines, and an uncaptured authorization never produces one.

One small part of the finding goes too far. The late response is "logged against the attempt," so some record does exist. The document still never treats it as a live authorization to track or reverse. The central premise holds.

data.doc_passage: Recovery point objective for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region. ... Aurora Global Database replicates the payments and ledger cluster to ap-southeast-3. Replication is storage-level and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second. • MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache are not replicated cross-region; on regional failover they are recreated empty in ap-southeast-3 from infrastructure-as-code, and in-flight idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings even if a whole region is lost, but Section 20.2 says the only cross-region copy (Aurora Global Database) is asynchronous with typical lag under one second, and says idempotency state is rebuilt from a payment table that (per Section 19) has no idempotency-key or request-hash column.
data.rationale: The document backs the finding's claims. NFR-4 requires zero RPO even if a whole region is lost. Section 20.2 says cross-region replication is asynchronous, with typical lag under one second. Section 20.2 also says idempotency state is rebuilt from the payment table after a regional failover. The Section 19 payment table has no idempotency_key or request_hash column. It does have merchant_account_id and merchant_reference, so the finding's claim that there is no "merchant_id" column is only literally true. The finding cites "AD-004", which does not appear anywhere in the document, but that label is not part of its central premise.

data.doc_passage:
CAPTURED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
SUCCEEDED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
SETTLED -> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 7.2 permits no transition from PARTIALLY_REFUNDED or REFUNDED to SETTLED and no CAPTURED to CAPTURED transition, even though Section 16.2 moves every matched payment to SETTLED. Section 8 also calls the authorization a ledger journal while Section 14.3 puts holds in a separate memo ledger, and Section 14.2 gives no refund or FX journal examples.
data.rationale: Section 7.2 lists PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED as the only transition out of PARTIALLY_REFUNDED. REFUNDED has no outgoing transitions. CAPTURED cannot move back to CAPTURED. Section 16.2 says "Matched payments transition to SETTLED". Step 10 of Section 8 reads "ledger journal (authorization memo)", while Section 14.3 says holds are "recorded as memo entries in a separate memo ledger, not in the financial ledger". Section 14.2 gives only capture, settlement and payout examples, with no refund or FX journals. Every factual part of the finding matches the document.

data.doc_passage: The batch matcher starts once all expected files for business day T have been received, so that cross-provider netting and multi-provider payouts are computed on a complete day. ... At 2025 volume, the matcher's measured end-to-end run time is 45 minutes, and merchant settlement report generation takes a further 15 minutes. [16.1: ACQ-TH1 CSV over SFTP Daily 06:30 ICT]
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 16.2 starts the matcher only once every file for day T has arrived, and has no cut-off or partial-run path. The latest file (ACQ-TH1) arrives at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT. Matching plus report generation takes 60 minutes at 2025 volume, so reports cannot be published by the 08:00 SGT deadline in NFR-8.
data.rationale: The finding's premise holds. Section 16.2 does make the matcher wait for every expected file. Section 16.1 lists ACQ-TH1 at 06:30 ICT (UTC+7), which is 07:30 SGT (UTC+8). Section 16.2 gives 45 minutes for matching plus 15 for reports at 2025 volume, so the earliest publication is 08:30 SGT. NFR-8 requires 08:00 SGT. Volume roughly doubles from 2025 to 2027 (5.1M to 10.5M attempts per day). I found no cut-off or partial-run path for late or missing files anywhere in the document. One detail doesn't check out: the finding refers to "AD-016", which doesn't appear in the document. That label doesn't affect the central premise.

data.doc_passage: The Vault's KEKs are held in an AWS CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. CloudHSM takes automatic daily backups of the cluster to S3, from which a new HSM can be created in any AZ. A second HSM will be added to the cluster when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. If the HSM is unreachable, the Vault returns HTTP 503 and the Card Adapter maps this to a retryable outcome.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 12.3 puts all KEKs in a single CloudHSM in ap-southeast-1a and adds a second HSM only when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. At the design target, card volume is about 1,100 TPS (55% of 2,000), so that trigger never fires. DEKs are not cached, and a Vault 503 is mapped to a retryable outcome.
data.rationale: Each factual claim in the finding matches the document. Section 12.3 places a single HSM in ap-southeast-1a, sets the 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM, and maps a Vault 503 to a retryable outcome. Section 12.1 says DEKs are not cached and each detokenise call unwraps the DEK inside the HSM. Section 20.1 says services run across three AZs. Section 1 sets a peak of 2,000 TPS with a 55% card share, which gives about 1,100 card TPS. That is below the 1,500 TPS trigger.

data.doc_passage: A Finance or Owner user can change the payout bank account in the portal. The change takes effect from the next payout cycle. A confirmation email is sent to the user who made the change, and the change is written to the audit log.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 18.4 lets a Finance or Owner user change the payout bank account with no step-up MFA and no second approver, and sends the confirmation email only to the user who made the change. MFA is optional for the Finance role, and Finance can also issue refunds.
data.rationale: Section 18.4 says the confirmation email goes only to the user who made the change. It does not mention step-up MFA, a second approver, or notifying the Owner. Section 18.3 enforces TOTP only for the Owner role, and other roles "may enable it". Section 18.2 gives Finance both "Issue refunds" and "edit payout bank account". The only second-approver rule is in 18.5, and it covers internal back-office write actions, not merchant portal changes. The document contains nothing that adds these controls to payout account changes.

data.doc_passage:
8 Fraud Hook (FRV-1) Yes - vendor contract (Backlog item 4)
9 Hardening - load, chaos and DR game days; PCI DSS assessment; Section 26 test plan Follows Section 26
The first merchant cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) goes live after Phase 7; other markets follow at four-week intervals.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 28 sends the first Singapore card cohort live after Phase 7. That comes before Phase 8 (Fraud Hook, blocked on the FRV-1 contract) and Phase 9 (load tests, DR game days and the PCI DSS assessment), while FR-9 requires fraud scoring for every card payment. Section 27 says only the Admin API schemas and the dispute module are gaps, and neither blocks the first cohort.
data.rationale: Section 28 puts the go-live of the Singapore cards and PayNow cohort after Phase 7. The Fraud Hook is Phase 8 and depends on the FRV-1 vendor contract (Backlog item 4). The load tests, DR game days and PCI DSS assessment are all in Phase 9. FR-9 requires that every card payment be scored before authorization. Section 27 names only the Admin API schemas and the dispute module as material gaps and says neither blocks the first cohort; it does not mention the fraud, PCI or load/DR sequencing. The document also does not name anyone who accepts this risk.

data.doc_passage: Cascading does not move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade; the cascade path therefore sits above the 99th percentile. [§10.5: "retryable outcomes - soft declines eligible for reattempt plus acquirer-side errors and timeouts - 3.8%"; §26.2 NFR-2: "Under the NFR-1 load with 3.8% retryable-outcome injection, p99 end-to-end card authorization ≤ 1,500 ms"]
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 21.1 leaves cascades out of the p99 latency budget because "fewer than 1% of card payments cascade." This conflicts with the 3.8% retryable-outcome baseline in Section 10.5 and the 3.8% injection rate in the NFR-2 acceptance test, while NFR-2 itself counts any cascade and the retry timeout is 2,500 ms.
data.rationale:
The document contains every passage the finding quotes:
- **Section 21.1** says "fewer than 1% of card payments cascade."
- **Section 10.5** gives a 3.8% retryable baseline.
- **Section 26.2** injects 3.8% retryable outcomes in the NFR-2 test.
- **NFR-2** measures end-to-end latency "including any cascade."
- **Section 11.1** sets the retryable timeout at 2,500 ms, which is above the 1,500 ms target.
- **3DS** is a step in the Section 8 flow, but it is not a line in the Section 21.1 budget table or in NFR-2's wording.

Together, these passages back the finding's description of the document.

data.doc_passage: DynamoDB serves each partition key value from a single partition, and a single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units per second. Our largest merchant (marketplace M-0001) peaks at approximately 900 create-payment TPS during campaign events (45% of 2,000 TPS). Each request consumes two writes - lock acquisition and completion update - or about 1,800 WCU at peak, comfortably within the perpartition ceiling. Keying by merchant_id keeps each merchant's records co-located, which the local secondary index on created_at uses...
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 9.3 justifies keying the idempotency table on merchant_id by saying a single partition sustains 10,000 WCU/s and the largest merchant needs about 1,800 WCU (two writes per request). The finding says this count ignores item size, even though response_body can be up to 4 KB, and ignores any LSI item-collection constraint.
data.rationale: Section 9.3 says exactly what the finding quotes: 10,000 WCU per partition, two writes per request, and about 1,800 WCU at peak. The table in Section 9.2 lists response_body as "Serialised response, up to 4 KB", but the capacity math counts one WCU per write regardless of item size. The document also mentions the LSI on created_at without discussing any item-collection size limit. Whether the 10,000 WCU figure is actually correct is a question about AWS, not about what the document says. The document does make the statements the finding attributes to it and leaves out the factors the finding lists.

data.doc_passage: Token Requestor onboarding - Visa VTS and Mastercard MDES token-requestor registration (TRID) and the commercial agreement with a token service provider; certification test plan. Application not yet submitted.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 24 confirms VTS/MDES network tokens as the primary card-on-file credential from launch, and Phase 3, which includes card-on-file with network tokens, is rated 'No - ready'. Meanwhile Backlog item 2 says the Token Requestor registration, commercial agreement and certification have not started. The backlog item is not linked to the decision or the phase gate.
data.rationale: The document backs the finding's premise. Section 24 says "Network tokens (VTS/MDES) as the primary credential for all card-on-file and recurring payments from launch". Section 28 marks Phase 3 ("Transaction core ... card-on-file with network tokens") as "No - ready". Section 27 rates the Card Vault "Ready" because "network tokens [are] specified". Backlog item 2 still says the TRID application has not been submitted. Neither Section 27 nor Section 28 mentions Backlog item 2, and that item has no owner, date or fallback. The only PAN fallback the document describes is for issuers that don't support network tokens, not for a missing TRID. One small point: the document does not label the decision "AD-010", but the quoted text does appear in Section 24.

data.doc_passage: The Retry Engine maintains a per-card (PAN fingerprint) and per-merchant reattempt counter over a rolling 30-day window and stops reattempting at the scheme limits applicable to the card.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document says the Retry Engine stops at "the scheme limits applicable to the card", but it never gives those limits, never names the rule set they come from, and never says whether cascading a 05/91/96 decline to a different acquirer counts as a reattempt. Section 27 still rates the Retry Engine "Ready".
data.rationale: Section 11.3 says the Retry Engine stops "at the scheme limits applicable to the card" but gives no numbers and names no scheme rule document. Section 11.1 names Visa Category 1 and Mastercard Merchant Advice Codes 03 and 21 only as triggers for a final decline, not as limits. I found no text anywhere in the document that says whether a cascade to a different acquirer counts toward the reattempt counter. The FR-7 test in Section 26.1 checks against "scheme reattempt limits" without defining them. Section 27 rates the Retry Engine "Ready" and says the scheme rules are "specified (Section 11)". So the absence the finding describes is real.

data.doc_passage: Every 60 seconds, the Orchestrator's sweeper finds payments in AUTHORISING for more than 30 seconds, queries the provider's status endpoint where one exists, and resolves the payment to AUTHORISED or FAILED. Payments still unresolved after 10 minutes are escalated to the operations queue. The sweeper also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document leaves several idempotency failure paths unspecified: the stuck-payment sweeper only scans payments in AUTHORISING, so it does not cover IN_PROGRESS locks orphaned before a payment exists or while it is in CREATED; Section 20.4 does not address DynamoDB outage or throttling; and the risk of an order-ID key being reused after the 24-hour expiry is not discussed.
data.rationale: Section 9.2 says the sweeper recovers locks left IN_PROGRESS by crashed pods. Section 20.3's only stated scan condition is payments in AUTHORISING for more than 30 seconds. The section does add that the sweeper "also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS", so the finding slightly overstates how narrow it is. Still, the document never says how records are found or resolved when no payment exists yet or when the payment is in CREATED, and Section 9.2 assumes the sweeper "resolves the payment". The Section 20.4 degradation table covers a Redis outage but has no row for DynamoDB being unavailable or throttled, and I found no fail-open or fail-closed rule for that case anywhere. Section 9.1 accepts order or invoice IDs as keys and says a request after the 24-hour expiry "is treated as new". The document never discusses the duplicate-charge risk this creates for FR-5. The core claims hold.

data.doc_passage: Retention: payment and attempt records 7 years (financial records); idempotency records 24 hours; webhook events 30 days; raw settlement files 7 years in S3 Glacier.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document gives NFR-7 privacy obligations but never provides a field-level personal-data purpose and retention map, a data-subject request process, or a cross-border transfer basis or data-localisation position, while the only retention rules cover payment, idempotency, webhook and settlement records.
data.rationale: The document has no field-level purpose and retention map, no process for data-subject requests, and no legal basis for cross-border transfers. It also never addresses whether any market requires data to be processed locally. The only nearby text is the NFR-7 acceptance criterion in Section 26.2, which says a future DPO review will map every personal data field to a purpose and retention period. That sets a test, not a map. Section 14.3 mentions data-subject deletion requests only to say the ledger is unaffected. Section 13.1 confirms that device fingerprint, IP address, user agent, and hashed email and phone are sent to FRV-1, and Backlog item 4 confirms the FRV-1 data processing agreement is pending. Section 19.1 and Section 20 confirm that all data is in Singapore with disaster recovery in Jakarta. Two details are slightly off. First, the fraud payload sends only shipping and billing country, not full addresses. Second, audit records also have a stated retention period: five years under NFR-12. Neither detail changes the central claim.

data.doc_passage: FR-8: "...prefer the lowest-cost eligible acquirer unless doing so reduces the expected authorization rate by more than 2%." §10.3: "applies the cost preference when the difference is within the configured tolerance (default 2)." §24: "Weighted cost/approval/latency score; cost-preferred within 2 tolerance". §26.1 FR-8: "For a set of synthetic transactions with configured costs and approval priors, the selected acquirer matches the expected choice."
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document never says whether FR-8's '2%' and the routing 'tolerance (default 2)' mean percentage points or a relative percentage, and the FR-8 acceptance test checks only expected acquirer choices without testing the tolerance bound.
data.rationale: The finding's premise holds. FR-8 says "2%", while §10.3 and §24 give a tolerance of "2" with no unit. I found no passage that says whether this means percentage points or relative percent. §10.3 compares the lowest-cost acquirer with the highest-approval acquirer, and §10.2 ranks acquirers by a weighted score whose default emphasises cost, as the finding says. The FR-8 acceptance criterion checks only that the selected acquirer matches the expected one and never names the tolerance boundary. One detail is off: the "AD-012" label does not appear in the document. The same unitless tolerance is in the §24 Confirmed Decisions row, though, so this mislabel doesn't affect the central premise.

data.doc_passage: FR-5: "Send a create-payment request; after its response is received, resend the identical request with the same Idempotency-Key." (FR-5 itself says: "including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently"). FR-12: "Every state change emits exactly one event". Section 17: "Delivery. At-least-once." NFR-9: "One merchant at 3× its rate limit does not move other merchants' p99 by more than 5%."
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The FR-5 acceptance test resends only after the first response arrives, so it does not test concurrent duplicates. The FR-12 test expects 'exactly one event' per state change while Section 17 specifies at-least-once delivery. The NFR-9 test is measured against an unspecified rate limit with no baseline load level.
data.rationale: The document matches the finding on all three points. The FR-5 test resends only after the first response is received, but FR-5 explicitly requires correct handling of concurrent duplicates. The FR-12 test says "exactly one event", while Section 17 says delivery is at-least-once. The NFR-9 test is stated relative to "its rate limit", but Section 5 only says rate limits are configurable per merchant tier and gives no value. The test also sets no baseline load level. Whether "emits exactly one event" really conflicts with at-least-once delivery is the finding's own interpretation. Its description of the document's text is accurate.

data.doc_passage: The Payout Service computes each merchant account's payable balance after settlement, subtracts reserves and pending dispute holds, and instructs the sponsor bank by ISO 20022 pain.001 file or API. ... Payouts | Ready | Section 16.3.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document does not specify how the customer's nominated account for payout-based refunds is collected, verified or journaled. It also does not say how reserves and dispute holds are set, or what happens when merchant_payable goes negative, yet Section 27 rates Payouts 'Ready'.
data.rationale: The customer's nominated refund account appears only in FR-15, and the FR-15 test in Section 26 only checks that a payout instruction is produced. No section says how that account is collected, verified or protected, and none describes a journal for a refund payout. Section 14 lists a refund_clearing account, but none of the example journals uses it. Section 16.3 mentions reserves and pending dispute holds without saying how they are set. I found no rule anywhere for a negative merchant_payable. Section 27 rates Payouts 'Ready' and cites Section 16.3. One detail is off: the finding cites 'AD-020', an ID that does not appear in the document, where disputes are actually Backlog item 1. This does not change the central claim.

data.doc_passage: Last updated 2026-09-14 (architecture) · consolidated 2026-09-21 ... Companion documents MPOP Conceptual Design v1.2; PCI DSS Scoping Memo (draft); Acquirer Connectivity Matrix ... Separately, the weekly Routing Review compares each merchant's realised authorization rate under cost-preferred routing against a control slice (5% of traffic routed approval-first) and adjusts weights where the merchant's authorization rate has fallen by more than the tolerance.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document gives no named owner or SLA for its recurring human processes (the weekly Routing Review, the Finance Operations exception queue, paging and payout freezes on ledger discrepancies, DR rehearsals, the HSM capacity trigger), has no change log for the 2026-09-21 consolidation, and cites the PCI DSS Scoping Memo as a draft.
data.rationale:
I searched the whole document, and its main claims hold up:
- **Routing Review (10.3):** described with no owner or SLA.
- **DR rehearsals (20.2):** "rehearsed twice a year," with no owner given.
- **HSM capacity trigger (12.3):** "when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS" names no one responsible for adding the second HSM.
- **Ledger discrepancies (14.3):** the only response named is "pages the on-call engineer." No resolution owner or SLA is given.
- **Exceptions queue (16.2):** goes to a "Finance Operations queue," but no handling SLA is stated.
- **Title page:** shows the consolidation date but no change log or revision history. It does cite the PCI DSS Scoping Memo as a draft.

Two caveats:
- The document names teams in places: Finance Operations for the queue, and the "Payments Core Team" as author of the document. But it never assigns owners or SLAs for the processes themselves, so the finding's core claim still stands.
- The document never says outright that Section 12.2 depends on the draft memo. That link is the finding's inference, not something the text states.

items.rationale: Shows that §9.2 writes the response to idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, with no merchant_id in the key, for 24 hours, and that a hit returns before DynamoDB or the Orchestrator are touched.

Confirms Redis is checked first and a hit returns the stored response without touching DynamoDB. The passage also shows request_hash lives only in the DynamoDB table, so on a hit the hash comparison never runs.
§9.1 accepts merchants' own order or invoice identifiers as keys and says reuse with a different body should return HTTP 422. This is the contract the fast path skips.
P3 says idempotency is scoped to (merchant, key). A Redis key without merchant identity breaks this principle.

The cited passages establish the inference. The Redis key holds only the client key, order numbers are accepted as keys, a hit returns the stored response before DynamoDB, and the request_hash check exists only in DynamoDB. So two merchants using the same key share one entry, and a changed body gets the cached response instead of a 422. The claim's extra details (card BIN and last 4, FR-5) are not in these passages, but the inference does not rely on them.

The passage says the Fraud Hook gets the PAN through the Vault's detokenise operation, using the Card Adapter client library and service role. It also says FRV-1's velocity graph is keyed on the full card number, which shows the PAN goes to FRV-1. That establishes the Section 13.1 behaviour the claim describes.
Section 12.1 states plainly that only the Card Adapter's service identity may call detokenise. That is the rule the claim says is contradicted.
The Section 12.2 table lists the Fraud Hook as out of PCI DSS scope on the basis 'Token, BIN, last 4 only'. That is exactly the scoping the claim cites.
P2 says PAN never leaves the Vault boundary except over the Card Adapter's connection to an acquirer, and that all other services handle tokens only. This matches what the claim attributes to P2.

It shows the Card Adapter is in the CDE because it transmits PAN to acquirers. That is the scope basis behind the argument. On its own, though, it says nothing about the Fraud Hook or FRV-1, so it only supports the claim through the inference.

The source passages do support the step 'transmits PAN means CDE, so the Fraud Hook belongs in the CDE and the Section 12.2 table is wrong'. But none of the cited passages show that NFR-5 relies on or is assessed against the Section 12.2 boundary, so that link is assumed rather than established.

The passage states that on a retryable outcome the Retry Engine immediately submits a new attempt to the next acquirer. It also says responses arriving after the 2,500 ms timeout are logged against the attempt and discarded. That establishes the Section 11.2 discard-and-cascade part of the claim it is cited for.
The passage quotes the design's statement that 'cascading cannot create a duplicate charge: the ledger records only the approved attempt'. That establishes the assertion the claim goes on to dispute.
The Section 11.1 table lists 'no response within 2,500 ms' under Retryable, with the action 'Cascade to next candidate acquirer'. That establishes that a timeout is treated as retryable.

The passages establish that timeouts trigger a cascade and that late responses are discarded. They do not show that a timed-out attempt may have been approved; that rests on unstated domain knowledge. These short excerpts also cannot show that the whole design lacks a reversal or reconciliation. They partly undercut 'no record', because late responses are 'logged against the attempt'. P1 and P10 do not appear in any of the passages.

Section 20.2 says Aurora Global Database replication to ap-southeast-3 is asynchronous with typical lag under one second. It also says MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache are not replicated cross-region, which makes Aurora the only cross-region copy.

The passage states that RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region, under the NFR-4 row. The table layout is slightly garbled, but it reads as NFR-4.

The passage says that on regional failover, in-flight idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table, which is the part of the claim this item is cited for. It says nothing about which columns the Section 19 payment table has.

It shows the NFR-4 game day uses an unplanned Aurora failover and requires every posting committed before the failure to be present afterwards. It does not show that the test cannot pass. That depends on the asynchronous lag described in other passages.

EV-017 and EV-018 support the first inference: asynchronous replication with lag means RPO is above zero, which conflicts with NFR-4. The second inference, that the Section 19 payment table has no idempotency key or request hash column, is not backed by any cited passage, because the Section 19 schema is not included.
Section 16.2 says the batch matcher starts once all expected files for business day T have been received, which is the part of the claim this item is cited for.
The 16.1 intake table lists ACQ-TH1 as CSV over SFTP, delivered daily at 06:30 ICT.
The passage says that at 2025 volume the matcher's end-to-end run takes 45 minutes and report generation a further 15 minutes, so 60 minutes in total.
NFR-8 requires merchant settlement reports for day T to be published by 08:00 SGT on T+1. This is the deadline the claim measures against.
The volume baseline gives 5.1 M average daily attempts in 2025 and 10.5 M in 2027, which is about twice the 2025 level.

The arithmetic holds: 06:30 ICT plus the 1-hour offset is 07:30 SGT, and adding 60 minutes gives 08:30, past the 08:00 deadline. The UTC+7 and UTC+8 offsets are standard but don't appear in the passages. The inference also says the 2027 volume growth 'lengthens the run further', which assumes run time grows with volume; the source passages don't say that. The passages also don't cover the claim's points about there being no cut-off or partial-run path and about payouts (FR-17).

The passage says the Vault stores the CVC encrypted and deletes it at SETTLED or after 72 hours, whichever comes first. It names incremental authorizations as a use. It also states that PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow retention 'until the transaction is settled'. That fully establishes what the design asserts.

Section 12.4 lists incremental authorizations (ride-hailing tips, hotel extensions) among the reasons for keeping the CVC, separate from the initial customer-initiated authorization. It also gives the settlement-or-72-hours deletion rule. This establishes the stated uses it is cited for.

The requirement says SAD is handled under Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2: stored encrypted in the Vault and deleted when the associated payment settles. This establishes the settlement-retention requirement it is cited for. It says nothing about the 72-hour limit, which comes from 12.4. The layout is garbled, so the SAD text appears to belong to NFR-6, while NFR-5 covers CDE scope.
The document header lists the companion 'PCI DSS Scoping Memo (draft)', which directly establishes that the memo is still a draft.

The source passages separate the initial authorization from incremental authorizations and keep the CVC until settlement, so the design does depend on retention after authorization. Two points go beyond them. First, they don't say outright that incremental authorizations happen after the initial one completes; that comes from domain knowledge. Second, the claim that no register evidence confirms the reading is a statement about what is absent, and the cited passages can't show it. EV-016 only shows the memo is a draft.

The full 7.2 transition list has no PARTIALLY_REFUNDED/REFUNDED -> SETTLED edge. CAPTURED leads only to SETTLED, PARTIALLY_REFUNDED or REFUNDED, so there is no CAPTURED -> CAPTURED edge. That establishes the state-machine part of the claim.
The only exit from PARTIALLY_REFUNDED is to REFUNDED, and REFUNDED has no outgoing transitions. This confirms that neither refunded state can move to SETTLED.
Section 16.2 says plainly that matched payments transition to SETTLED. It also says unmatched or mismatched lines become exceptions. This is the part of the claim the item is cited for.
FR-1 requires capture (full and partial). FR-2 allows only the transitions listed in Section 7. These are the two requirements the claim relies on.
Step 10 records the authorization outcome with a 'ledger journal (authorization memo)', matching the claim's quote from Section 8.
Section 14.3 says authorization holds are memo entries in a separate memo ledger, not the financial ledger. That is the contrast the claim draws.

The sources do establish four things: CAPTURED -> REFUNDED/PARTIALLY_REFUNDED is allowed, neither refunded state can go to SETTLED, matching moves payments to SETTLED, and FR-2 forbids unlisted transitions. They also show there is no CAPTURED -> CAPTURED edge. But they don't say what happens when a matched payment can't legally move to SETTLED. Section 16.2 sends only unmatched or mismatched lines to exceptions, so 'falls into exceptions' (and the NFR-8 impact) is an assumption.
The passage says the first cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) goes live after Phase 7. It lists the Fraud Hook as Phase 8 and hardening as Phase 9, so the launch-after-Phase-7 part is established.

Phase 8 is the Fraud Hook (FRV-1). Its dependency entry reads 'Yes - vendor contract (Backlog item 4)'. Compared with the other rows ('No - ready', 'Partially - ... outstanding'), this shows it is blocked on the vendor contract.
Phase 9 is listed as 'Hardening - load, chaos and DR game days; PCI DSS assessment; Section 26 test plan', which establishes that these happen in Phase 9.
FR-9 states that every card payment shall be scored by the fraud-scoring hook before authorization, which establishes the requirement the claim cites.

The cited passages show that go-live follows Phase 7, ahead of the Fraud Hook (Phase 8) and the PCI DSS assessment and load/DR work (Phase 9). Together with FR-9, that supports live cards running without fraud scoring. However, none of the passages defines NFR-5 as the PCI DSS requirement or NFR-1/2/4 as the targets the load/DR tests demonstrate, so that mapping is an unstated assumption. The inference also does not cover the claims about Section 27 or the missing risk owner.
Section 12.3 says the KEKs are held in a CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. It also gives the 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM and says a 503 is mapped to a retryable outcome.
The passage states that a second HSM is added only above sustained card volume of 1,500 TPS, and that an unreachable HSM leads to a Vault 503, which the Card Adapter maps to a retryable outcome.
The volume baseline gives a design-target peak of 2,000 TPS and a 55% card share. These are the inputs for the 1,100 TPS figure.
Section 20.1 states that every service runs at least three replicas spread across three AZs. This is the contrast the claim draws with the single-AZ HSM.

The passage says each detokenise call unwraps the DEK inside the HSM and that DEKs are not cached. It also says each record's DEK is wrapped by a KEK held in CloudHSM. Together these establish that tokenise and detokenise both depend on the HSM.

The cited passages establish the arithmetic: 55% of 2,000 is 1,100, below the 1,500 trigger. With one HSM in a single AZ, per-call DEK unwrapping and no caching, every card payment depends on the HSM. Because every cascade candidate needs detokenise through the same Vault, a 503 makes all of them fail. The inference matches the part of the claim it is cited for. The per-card reattempt counters, the restore-from-backup outage and NFR-3 are not part of what it is cited for.
Section 18.4 says that a Finance or Owner user can change the payout bank account in the portal, which is exactly what this item is cited for.
Section 18.4 says the confirmation email goes to the user who made the change, and no other recipient is named. Besides that email, the change is only written to the audit log.
Section 18.3 enforces TOTP only for the Owner role. Other roles, including Finance, 'may enable it', so MFA is optional for Finance.
The Section 18.2 roles table gives Finance both 'Issue refunds' and 'edit payout bank account', which supports the claim that Finance holds refund rights as well as payout-account control.

The passage states P9 directly: 'money-moving permissions are separated from configuration permissions.' This is the principle the claim says is violated. The conflict itself comes from combining P9 with EV-040.

The cited passages support that a Finance user without MFA can change the payout account, effective from the next cycle, and that the only email goes to that user's account. They do not support the claim that 'the only alert goes to the attacker'. A phished password does not give access to the victim's email inbox, so the legitimate user may still get the confirmation. The audit log is also written, though it is not described as an alert.

Section 21.1 says cascading 'does not move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade' and leaves the cascade path out of the 1,338 ms budget. The budget rows it lists (routing, vault, acquirer, commit, response) include no 3DS line.

Section 10.5 says retryable outcomes (soft declines plus acquirer errors and timeouts) are 3.8% of card attempts, which contradicts the '<1%' assumption. One nuance: the figure is per attempt, not per payment.
NFR-2 says p99 end-to-end card authorization 'including any cascade' shall not exceed 1,500 ms. Its wording does not mention 3DS.
The NFR-2 acceptance test runs with 3.8% retryable-outcome injection and requires p99 ≤ 1,500 ms.
A retryable timeout is defined as no response within 2,500 ms. By simple arithmetic, any payment whose attempt times out takes longer than 1,500 ms.

The cited passages establish the contradiction between '<1%' and 3.8%, and that any payment with a timed-out attempt exceeds 1,500 ms. But saying cascaded payments necessarily 'set the p99' assumes they are among the slowest 1%. Soft declines can come back quickly, so some cascades may still finish under 1,500 ms. The passages also do not say what share of the 3.8% is timeouts, so 'fails if timeouts exceed ~1%' stays conditional. The inference does not address the 3DS part of the claim.

Section 9.3 says a single partition sustains up to 10,000 WCU per second and that each partition key value is served from a single partition. This is the assumption the claim says the merchant_id key relies on.

The passage states two writes per request (lock acquisition and completion update), about 1,800 WCU at peak for M-0001 at 900 TPS, which is 45% of 2,000 TPS. It also shows the count is per request with no mention of item size.
The table schema lists response_body as a serialised response of up to 4 KB, which establishes the item-size point.
The passage confirms there is an LSI on created_at under the merchant_id partition key. It says nothing about an item-collection size constraint, so that part depends on outside DynamoDB knowledge.

The cited passages establish the 10,000 WCU assumption, the two-write count, the 4 KB response_body and the LSI. Per-KB charging and the LSI limit are only conditional ('if'), not established. Nothing in the passages supports the throttling, failed-payment or NFR-1/NFR-3 consequences.

The passage states that a lock left IN_PROGRESS by a crashed pod is recovered by the stuck-payment sweeper (Section 20.3), and that IN_PROGRESS returns 409. This establishes the part of the claim about Section 9.2 relying on the sweeper.

The passage confirms the sweeper finds payments in AUTHORISING. However, it also says 'The sweeper also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS', which does not tie that cleanup to AUTHORISING payments. So the passage does not show that the sweeper scans only AUTHORISING payments, or that locks from pre-payment or CREATED crashes are left behind. The claim needs the unstated assumption that IN_PROGRESS cleanup only happens through payment resolution.

The passage says merchants' order or invoice identifiers are accepted as keys, records are kept for 24 hours, and 'A request after expiry is treated as new.' Together these establish that a retry with the same order ID after expiry would create a new (second) payment.

The dependency-degradation table lists acquirer, fraud vendor, Redis and MSK failures, and then Section 21 begins. It has no row for DynamoDB being down or throttled. This shows Redis outage is covered but DynamoDB unavailability is not, so the fail-open or fail-closed behaviour is undefined.

The source passages support the DynamoDB half of the inference: no DynamoDB failure behaviour is defined. The sweeper half overreaches. EV-055 states the sweeper 'also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS' without limiting this to AUTHORISING payments, so the sources do not establish that locks taken before a payment exists, or during CREATED or REQUIRES_ACTION, cannot be resolved.

Backlog item 2 lists VTS/MDES TRID registration, the commercial agreement with a token service provider and a certification test plan as pending, and says 'Application not yet submitted'. No owner, date or fallback appears in the item. This establishes the backlog part of the claim.

The decision table says network tokens (VTS/MDES) are the primary credential for all card-on-file and recurring payments from launch, with PAN as a fallback only where the issuer doesn't support tokens. This establishes the decision part of the claim.
The Build Phases table, though its layout is garbled, shows Phase 3 (transaction core; card-on-file with network tokens) marked 'No - ready'. This establishes the readiness-rating part of the claim.

The cited passages establish the inference: a confirmed 'from launch' decision and a 'ready' phase depend on a TRID application that hasn't been submitted. But the claim goes further. It says both will be false at launch and that all card-on-file traffic will fall back to PAN. No passage gives a launch date or onboarding lead time, and none says what happens when there is no TRID, so that conclusion rests on unstated assumptions.

This passage shows that Section 11.3 stops reattempting 'at the scheme limits applicable to the card' and gives no number or rule source in this excerpt. A single excerpt cannot prove the document never states the limits anywhere. It also says nothing about whether a cascade on codes 05, 91 or 96 counts as a reattempt, about the register, or about fines.

The readiness table rates the Retry Engine 'Ready' because 'Outcome classes, cascade limits and scheme rules [are] specified (Section 11)'. That establishes the 'still rates Ready' part. The section number (27) isn't visible in the excerpt, but the content clearly matches the claim.
FR-7 requires that cascades 'stop at scheme reattempt limits', which establishes that the FR-7 test checks those limits.

The cited passages show that the limits are referred to but not defined in these excerpts, so the inference is plausible. It assumes, without showing it, that the limits and rule source appear nowhere else in the document. It also doesn't address the cascade/reattempt question, the register evidence, or the fines risk.

The payload table confirms that device fingerprint, IP address, user agent, SHA-256 email and phone, and shipping/billing country go to FRV-1. The claim says 'addresses', but the passage lists only the countries. It also says nothing about the DPA status, bank accounts for refunds or where data is processed.

NFR-7 explicitly requires processing under the five named laws (SG PDPA 2012, MY PDPA 2010, ID Law 27/2022, TH PDPA 2019, PH DPA 2012), including purpose limitation, retention limits and access logging.

It places all primary data stores in ap-southeast-1 (the Singapore region) and uses the Jakarta secondary for DR only. Its retention rules cover only payment and attempt records, idempotency records, webhook events and settlement files, which matches the claim's retention scope.
It lists the FRV-1 data processing agreement and SLA finalisation as an open item, which supports the claim that the FRV-1 DPA is pending.

Read with EV-066, the source passages do show that no retention rule covers the fields sent to FRV-1, and EV-067 shows the DPA is pending. But EV-064 does give a purpose for each field (e.g. Device signals, Identity linkage), which contradicts 'no stated purpose'. None of the passages mention data held for refunds (bank accounts) or a DPO sign-off, and none show that a transfer basis is missing.

FR-8 explicitly states the Routing Engine prefers the lowest-cost eligible acquirer unless doing so reduces the expected authorization rate by more than 2%, which is exactly what the claim attributes to FR-8.

Section 10.3 compares the approval prior of the lowest-cost acquirer with that of the highest-approval acquirer, against a unitless 'configured tolerance (default 2)'. The passage also notes that weights default to emphasising cost. This establishes the 10.3 part of the claim. AD-012 is not shown in the passage.
The FR-8 Routing decision test only checks that the selected acquirer matches the expected choice for synthetic transactions. Nothing in it probes the tolerance bound.

The source passages do establish that FR-8 says '2%' while 10.3 uses a unitless 'default 2', so the unit ambiguity holds and the arithmetic is correct. However, the 88% baseline does not appear in any cited passage. Also, 10.3 says the cost-preferred ranking is 'subject to FR-8', which suggests the bound is enforced. So the claim that the weighted score could go beyond the bound is plausible but not established.

FR-15 says that where a method has no refund API, the refund is executed as a bank payout to the customer's nominated account. That is the part of the claim this passage is cited for. It says nothing about how that account is collected, verified or protected, but those are absence claims this passage isn't cited to prove.

The passage contains all of Section 16.3 (it runs up to the start of Section 17). It subtracts 'reserves and pending dispute holds' without saying how they are set, and it has no rule for a negative payable balance. That establishes the Section 16.3 part of the claim.
The readiness table rates Payouts 'Ready', citing Section 16.3, and lists Disputes as 'Not ready' (Backlog item 1). This directly supports the claim that Section 27 rates Payouts 'Ready'.

The passages show these gaps only within FR-15 and Section 16.3. They don't show that no other section defines reserve and hold amounts, negative-balance handling or how the refund account is captured. The inference also leaves out the payout-journaling gap. So it supports the claim only on the unstated assumption that the rest of the document is silent too.
Confirms the FR-5 test resends only after the first response is received (sequential). The passage doesn't show that FR-5 explicitly names concurrent duplicates or cross-merchant key reuse.
Confirms the FR-12 test expects 'exactly one event' per state change. It doesn't mention at-least-once delivery, and it describes emission rather than delivery, so no conflict is shown here alone.
Quotes the NFR-9 test (3x rate limit, 5% p99), which gives no baseline load level. It can't show the rate limit is unspecified elsewhere, and says nothing about NFR-4.
States 'Delivery. At-least-once.', which supports the claim that the spec defines at-least-once webhook delivery. The section number isn't shown but is minor.

The sequential-replay point is supported by EV-071. But 'emits exactly one event' (emission) doesn't contradict at-least-once delivery, since one event can be delivered several times. It also assumes FR-5 names concurrent duplicates, which no quoted passage shows.

The title page shows the 2026-09-21 consolidation and lists the PCI DSS Scoping Memo as a draft. The excerpt does not show that no change log exists or that Section 12.2 depends on the memo. It also says nothing about owners or SLAs for the recurring processes.

The passage confirms a weekly Routing Review that adjusts routing weights. It names no owner or SLA, but a short excerpt cannot prove that none exists anywhere in the document. It does not cover the other processes in the claim.

The passage confirms that reconciliation exceptions go to the Finance Operations queue, with no owner or turnaround target stated here. That absence in one excerpt does not show the whole document lacks them. The passage does not cover paging, payout freezes, DR rehearsals or the HSM trigger.

The source passages show the Routing Review and the Finance Operations queue with no owner or SLA in the quoted text. The inference that none exists relies on an unstated assumption that these excerpts are complete. The claim that changes are untraceable is not established, because no passage shows a change log is missing. The inference also leaves out paging, payout freezes, DR rehearsals, the HSM capacity trigger and the Section 12.2 dependency.
